title: Generation of Synthetic Populations in Social Simulations: A Review of Methods and Practices
publisher: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation 25(2) 6 (Chapuis, Taillandier, Drogoul)

key_points.claim: Scope: agent population/attribute generation (not spatial placement or social network generation). Trend from simple KISS models toward data-driven KIDS models.
key_points.evidence_quote: does not consider the spatialization of those entities or generation of the social networks that connect them

key_points.claim: Definition and core challenge: a synthetic population is a simplified microscopic representation of the target population, matched to aggregate statistics. Problems are data incompleteness, inconsistency, and choosing indicators.
key_points.evidence_quote: a synthetic population is never identical to the target population, but designed to match various aggregate statistical measures of the target population

key_points.claim: Methods are classified into two paradigms: synthetic reconstruction (SR: draw attributes from estimated distributions, e.g. IPF, MCMC, copulas, Bayesian networks) and combinatorial optimization (CO: reweight or replicate real records). Hybrids are common.
key_points.evidence_quote: we set the distinguishing criterion as the synthesis technique to either create the properties of the entities or reproduce known real entities, termed as synthetic reconstruction (SR) and combinatorial optimization (CO)

key_points.claim: Hybrid and recent techniques: SR combined with CO, re-weighting, copula functions, hierarchical mixtures. Multilevel populations (individuals in households) are also supported.
key_points.evidence_quote: use CO techniques to mix SR-based synthetic populations at several scales

key_points.claim: Input data types: aggregate tables, microdata samples (typically 1–10% of the population), surveys and others. Samples are limited in scope.
key_points.evidence_quote: individual records of 1%, 2%, 5%, and in rare cases, 10% or more of the population

key_points.claim: Validation: quality is usually assessed against the same dataset used for generation, using distance indicators (TAE, SRMSE, RSSZ, etc.). This is a weakness.
key_points.evidence_quote: the quality of the synthetic population is assessed using the same dataset that has been used for the generation process

key_points.claim: Corpus: 478 JASSS articles from 2011 to 2021, of which 342 featured a simulation model.
key_points.evidence_quote: This range involved 478 articles spread over 40 issues, among which 342 featured a simulation model.

key_points.claim: Practice: most models use generic initialization. Random functions are used in 62%, constants in 33%, SR in about 12.6%, raw data in 9%, calibration in 3.8%, CO in 0.6%.
key_points.evidence_quote: 2 of 3 models relied on a generic random function, such as uniform or normal distribution, and 1 inn 3 models relied on a constant value. SR techniques were used in more than 12% of the models

key_points.claim: Most models use no empirical data for agent attributes.
key_points.evidence_quote: 191 models (55.85%) did not use any source of data to inform agent attribute generation

key_points.claim: Models tied to real-world applications or GIS data use SR more often (21.7% and 25%). Only about 22% of models use dedicated generation algorithms.
key_points.evidence_quote: On average 29.17% of the published models used conventional data regarding the target population, and only 22% relied on dedicated algorithm

key_points.claim: Reporting: the ODD protocol is insufficient to document how populations are initialized. The authors recommend ODD plus source code as a minimum standard.
key_points.evidence_quote: the ODD is generally not enough to be able to understand how agent populations are initialized in the models

key_points.claim: Explanations for low uptake: tools are hard to find and adapt, are not integrated into modelling platforms, and there is a lack of data on abstract attributes such as attitudes and mental states.
key_points.evidence_quote: the abstract attributes related to social attitudes and mental states render it impossible to consider all agent attributes using the current synthetic population generation procedure

key_points.claim: Limitation: the review covers JASSS only. Transport modelling, which strongly influences population synthesis, is under-represented, so results may not generalize.
key_points.evidence_quote: outcomes from practices in JASSS cannot be generalized to ABM

reliability_notes: Full text obtained (23-page peer-reviewed PDF). Review of methods and of practice within JASSS 2011–2021 only, and not a fully systematic review. Covers only the population/attribute aspect, not networks, space, or cognition.
